title: Introduction and learning objectives for cancer causation
why: The lecturer introduces herself, the cancer lecture series, and the key learning outcomes for the session.

title: Cancer as clonal evolution in a permissive microenvironment
why: The lecturer explains how cancer develops through accumulated mutations and micro-evolution within a supportive tissue microenvironment.

title: Endogenous mutations, environmental exposures and inherited cancer susceptibility
why: The lecturer outlines the endogenous metabolic causes of DNA damage, inherited predisposition syndromes, and the role of target cell lifespan.

title: Established and suspected environmental cancer risks
why: The lecturer discusses common environmental carcinogen exposures, public perceptions of risk, and geographical differences revealed by epidemiology.

title: The cancer bad luck hypothesis and public interpretation
why: It examines the Tomasetti and Vogelstein hypothesis attributing cancer to random endogenous mutations versus environmental causes and discusses public reactions to it.

title: Geographic cancer incidence as evidence for environmental and genetic influences
why: It explores how worldwide geographic differences and migrant studies in epidemiology help distinguish environmental factors from genetic predispositions.

title: Infectious agents and their mechanisms of carcinogenesis
why: The lecturer surveys various bacteria, parasites, and viruses that contribute to cancer through chronic inflammation or cell cycle disruption.

title: Burkitt lymphoma: discovery, EBV, malaria and MYC translocation
why: The lecturer details Denis Burkitt's epidemiological discoveries and the mechanism by which malaria and EBV cooperate to drive Myc translocations.

title: Dietary aflatoxin activation and DNA adduct formation
why: The lecturer explains how dietary aflatoxin from Aspergillus is converted by liver oxidases into reactive DNA adducts.

title: UV-induced thymine dimers and nucleotide excision repair
why: The lecturer explains how ultraviolet radiation directly damages DNA by inducing thymine dimers that challenge nucleotide excision repair.

title: Benzo[a]pyrene metabolism, DNA adducts and transversion mutations
why: The lecturer describes how benzo[a]pyrene and TCDD activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor pathway to produce reactive epoxides and oxidative stress.

title: TCDD-induced oxidative stress and indirect DNA damage
why: The lecturer takes up a distinct chemical agent, TCDD, detailing its background in Agent Orange and explaining its mechanism of generating reactive oxygen species via the aryl hydrocarbon receptor.

title: Bladder-specific activation of carcinogenic aromatic amines
why: The lecturer explains why beta-naphthylamine specifically causes bladder cancer due to local enzymatic reactivation by urinary glucuronidase.

title: Asbestos-induced chronic inflammation and tumour promotion
why: The lecturer explains how inhaled asbestos fibers induce chronic inflammation in the mesothelium to promote tumor outgrowth without directly damaging DNA.

title: Experimental tumour initiation and promotion by DMBA and TPA
why: The lecturer explains the Berenbaum initiator-promoter model and details how TPA mimics diacylglycerol to activate protein kinase C.

title: Developmental stage and tissue susceptibility to carcinogens
why: The lecturer explains how alkylating agents and carcinogenic exposures have heightened effects during specific developmental windows of active proliferation.

title: Summary of DNA damage, tumour promotion and carcinogen specificity
why: The lecturer takes stock and summarizes the various direct and indirect mechanisms of DNA damage, metabolism, promotion, and tissue or life-stage specificities covered in the lecture.

title: Mutational signatures as evidence of carcinogen exposure
why: The lecturer explains how characteristic mutational signatures in sequenced cancer genomes can identify the specific carcinogens responsible for DNA damage.

title: Investigating carcinogenicity through epidemiology, exposure biomarkers and biobanks
why: The lecturer outlines the methods, biomarkers, and practical limitations of using population biobanks and animal models to test carcinogenicity.

title: Animal carcinogenicity studies: dose and species limitations
why: The lecturer moves from epidemiological approaches and biobanks to animal in vivo toxicity testing, explaining its protocols, limitations, and dosage issues.

title: The Ames mutagenicity test and its limitations
why: The lecturer explains the bacterial Ames test methodology and its use of liver extracts to assess direct and metabolized mutagens.

title: Lecture summary: environmental cancer risks, carcinogen assessment and risk–benefit decisions
why: The lecturer concludes the lecture with a summary of environmental carcinogenesis and the personal risk-benefit balances involved.
